questions.q: A student says: "When my father gives me ₹500 as pocket money, that's a business transaction because money changed hands." Is the student correct? Explain why or why not using the definition of a business transaction.
questions.a: No, the student is incorrect. A business transaction must involve an exchange between a business entity and another party that changes the financial position of the business. Pocket money is a personal gift within a family — no business entity is involved, no goods/services are exchanged for business purposes, and it doesn't affect a firm's assets, liabilities, or capital. This error reveals the student confuses any money transfer with a business transaction, missing the organizational and economic-exchange criteria.

questions.q: A shopkeeper sells goods worth ₹2,000 to a customer on credit. No invoice is issued, but the shopkeeper records it in a personal diary from memory. Is the diary entry a valid source document? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, the diary entry is not a valid source document. Source documents must be original, objective, verifiable records created at the time of the transaction (e.g., sales invoice, cash memo). A personal diary entry from memory lacks objectivity, is not independently verifiable, and can be altered — violating the evidentiary purpose of source documents. This misconception shows the student thinks any written record qualifies, not understanding the legal and audit requirements of authenticity and contemporaneity.

questions.q: Identify the source document for each: (a) Business deposits ₹50,000 cash into bank. (b) Business buys furniture on credit from M/s Delhi Furnishers. (c) Business pays ₹15,000 salary via cheque. (d) Business returns defective goods to supplier.
questions.a: (a) Pay-in-slip (bank deposit slip) — evidences cash deposited into bank. (b) Purchase invoice (received from supplier) — evidences credit purchase. (c) Cheque counterfoil or bank statement entry — evidences payment by cheque. (d) Debit note (issued by buyer to supplier) — evidences return of goods. If a student confuses (a) with cash memo or (d) with credit note, they misunderstand the direction and purpose of each document — a common error in distinguishing buyer- vs seller-initiated documents.

questions.q: Compare and contrast a source document and an accounting voucher. Give one example where a voucher is prepared *without* an external source document.
questions.a: A source document is the original evidence of a transaction created by the parties involved (e.g., invoice from supplier). An accounting voucher is an internal document prepared by the firm *based on* the source document to authorize and record the entry. Example: Petty cash expenses like auto-rickshaw fare (₹80) where no receipt is given — the firm prepares a petty cash voucher internally, approved by a manager. If a student says "voucher comes first," they reverse the causality: source document → voucher → journal entry.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "A transaction without a source document cannot be recorded in the books of accounts." Is it always true? Justify with a Class 11-level example.
questions.a: The statement is generally true but has an exception. Normally, no entry without a source document (verifiable evidence). However, for petty expenses (e.g., ₹50 for refreshments) where no external document exists, the firm prepares an *internal voucher* (approved by authority) which then acts as the source document. So the corrected principle: "Every recorded transaction must be supported by a source document — either external (invoice, cheque) or internal (approved voucher)." A student who says "always true" misses the internal voucher exception; one who says "never true" ignores the evidentiary foundation of accounting.

questions.q: Create a realistic scenario of a business transaction involving three parties where *two different source documents* are generated for the *same economic event* from different perspectives. Name the documents and explain why both are needed.
questions.a: Scenario: M/s Sharma Traders (buyer) orders goods from M/s Gupta Wholesalers (seller). M/s Gupta delivers goods via M/s Speedy Transport (carrier). Two source documents: (1) **Sales Invoice** from M/s Gupta to M/s Sharma — records sale, amount, GST. (2) **Lorry Receipt (LR)** from M/s Speedy Transport to M/s Gupta — evidences dispatch, enables buyer to claim goods. Both are needed: invoice for accounting/tax, LR for logistics/title transfer. A good answer shows understanding that one event (delivery) generates multiple documents for different purposes (legal, accounting, operational). A poor answer gives only one document or confuses perspectives.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A business ______ is an economic event involving the exchange of goods, services, or assets between two parties that can be measured in monetary terms and changes the financial position of the business.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you go to a stationery shop and buy a ______ for ₹50, paying by UPI.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you go to a stationery shop and buy a notebook for ₹______, paying by UPI.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to identify whether a given real-life event qualifies as a business transaction by applying the criteria of monetary measurability, two-party exchange, and financial position change, and must correctly match at least five common business activities to their appropriate source documents (e.g., cash sale → cash.
